title: Is It a Perfect Square
statement:
Given a positive integer num, return true if it equals k × k for some whole number k, and false otherwise.

Do not use a built-in square root or power function. Work it out with integer arithmetic.

examples.why: 18 × 18 = 324 and 19 × 19 = 361, so 360 falls between two squares.
The largest input. 46340² = 2147395600 is just below it and 46341² is just above. Squaring a guess near the top can overflow in languages with 32-bit ints.

hints: If num is a square, its root lies somewhere between 1 and num. Does k × k grow in a way you can search?
k × k only increases with k. Binary search on k and compare k × k with num.
Keep the upper bound small: the root of any allowed input is at most 46341, which also keeps k × k far from overflow.

explain.intuition:
The function k → k × k is increasing. So the question "is there a k with k × k = num?" is a search in a sorted list of squares, and binary search finds the answer in about 16 steps instead of up to 46 000.

The trap is overflow. In Java or C++ with 32-bit ints, mid * mid overflows once mid passes 46340. In JavaScript, numbers stay exact only up to 2⁵³, so very large mids lose precision. Capping the search at 46341 (or comparing mid with num / mid) avoids both.
steps: While lo ≤ hi, let mid be the middle and sq = mid × mid.
If sq === num, return true. If sq < num, set lo = mid + 1; otherwise hi = mid − 1.
pitfalls: Searching up to num itself and squaring huge mids, which overflows in 32-bit languages.
Using lo < hi and forgetting to check the last candidate, which misses 1 and other small squares.
Comparing floats from a square root call. Rounding can turn a near-square into a false positive.

solutions.title: Count up until the square passes num
solutions.idea: Try k = 1, 2, 3 … until k × k reaches or passes num.

solutions.title: Binary search on the root
solutions.idea: k × k is increasing in k, so binary search for a k whose square equals num.

solutions.title: Newton's method on integers
solutions.idea: Start at num and repeat x = (x + num / x) / 2 with integer division. It drops quickly to the floor of the square root.

followups: Return the floor of the square root instead of a yes/no answer.
Odd numbers 1, 3, 5, … add up to consecutive squares. How would you use that, and how fast is it?
